problems.problem: It is known that the number $\overline{a_1a_2a_3a_4a_5a_6}$ is divisible by $37$. Is it necessary that $\overline{a_2a_3a_4a_5a_6a_1}$ is also divisible by $37$?

Two circles $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ are tangent internally to the circle $\omega$ at points $A$ and $B$ ($AB$ is not a diameter of $\omega$) and intersect each other at points $C$ and $D$. Lines $AB$ and $CD$ are perpendicular. Prove that the radii of the circles $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ are equal.

Determine the maximum number of positive integers that can be made from the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$ such that no number contains repeated digits and any two of them have at most one common digit.
Find all positive integers that are $2000$ times bigger than the sum of their digits in decimal representation.
Find all integers $n$ such that $n^2+19n+99$ is a perfect square.

Prove that for positive numbers $a$ and $b$:
$$\frac{1}{a^3}+\frac{1}{3a^2b}+\frac{1}{3ab^2}+\frac{1}{b^3}\geqslant \frac{64}{3(a+b)^3}.$$

The triangle $ABC$ is given. The points in which the extensions of the medians of $ABC$ meet the circumcircle of this triangle are the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Prove that $ABC$ is also equilateral.
Find all values of the parameter $a$ such that the intersection of the figure given on the plane by $|x|+|y-a|\leqslant 2$ and the line $y=2001$ is a segment of length greater than $1$.

There are $13$ metro stations in the city, and three ring lines pass through them. Each ring line passes through all stations exactly once. Movement on each line is two-way. Any two stations are directly connected by at least one section of the underground track. Transfers are allowed at all stations.
a) Prove that there is a subway.
b) Prove that you can reach any station from any other by visiting at most one intermediate station.

On the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$, the points $M$ and $N$ are taken so that $MA=NB$. Prove that there is a point other than the point $B$ through which all circumcircles of the triangles $BMN$ pass.

Let $S(n)$ denote the sum of the digits in the decimal notation of $n$. Are there any positive integers $k$, $l$, $m$ such that $\frac{k+l+m}{3}$ is an integer and $S(k+l)<150$, $S(l+m)<150$, $S(m+k)<150$, $S\left(\frac{k+l+m}{3}\right)>2001$?
Prove that there are infinitely many quadruples of positive integers $k$, $l$, $m$, $n$ such that $k^2+l^4+m^5=n^{2001}$.

All five-digit numbers whose digits are in strictly increasing order from left to right are written on the board. Is it possible to cross out one digit from each of them so that all four-digit numbers with the same property are formed?

In triangle $ABC$, $I$ is the intersection point of the bisectors $AA_1$ and $CC_1$, and $M$ is an arbitrary point of the side $AC$. The lines parallel to these bisectors and passing through the point $M$ intersect the segments $AA_1$, $CC_1$, $AB$ and $CB$ at points $H$, $N$, $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Let $BC=a$, $AC=b$, $AB=c$ and let $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_3$ be the distances from the points $H$, $I$, $N$ to the line $PQ$ respectively. Prove that
$$\frac{d_1}{d_2}+\frac{d_2}{d_3}+\frac{d_3}{d_1}\geqslant \frac{2ab}{a^2+bc}+\frac{2ca}{c^2+ab}+\frac{2bc}{b^2+ca}.$$

Find all real values $a$ such that the system of equations
$$\begin{cases}(y-|x|)(x-a)=0,\\ x^2+y^2=1\end{cases}$$
has exactly three solutions.

Prove the inequality for positive $x$, $y$, $z$:
$$\frac{x^3+y^3}{x^2+y^2}+\frac{y^3+z^3}{y^2+z^2}+\frac{z^3+x^3}{z^2+x^2}\geqslant x+y+z.$$

Let the point $K$ lie on the side $AB$ of triangle $ABC$, and let the segment $CK$ intersect its bisector $BF$ at a point $Q$ such that $\angle BQC=2\angle BFA$ and $\angle BAF=2\angle CQF$. Prove that $KF=FC$.

An infinite (in all directions) sheet of paper with a square grid is given. Is it possible to write an integer in each cell so that all integers are written, each of them only once, in each column there is a number less than all other numbers of this column, and in each row there is a number greater than all other numbers of this row?

In the acute triangle $ABC$, $\angle ABC=60^\circ$, and $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ are its altitudes. On the rays $B_1A_1$ and $B_1C_1$ the points $N$ and $M$ are marked respectively, so that they lie outside the triangle $ABC$ and $NA_1=A_1C_1=C_1M$. Prove that the points $N$, $B$, $M$ are collinear.
Find all positive integers $k<2002$ such that $5n^7+7n^5+kn$ is divisible by $35$ for all positive integers $n$.

What is the smallest number of five-cell pieces of the form shown in the figure that can be cut out of an $8\times8$ board so that no such piece can be cut from the rest of that board?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ua9_2002_p7_fig.png

The set of numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2001, 2002$ is divided into two groups. The first group includes all the numbers with an odd sum of digits, and the second those with an even sum of digits. Find the difference between the sum of the numbers of the first group and the sum of the numbers of the second group.

Solve the equation
$$\left[x^3\right]=[3x+2]+\{x+2003\},$$
where $[a]$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $a$, $\{a\}=a-[a]$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers satisfying the inequality
$$ab>2002a+2003b.$$
Prove that
$$a+b>\left(\sqrt{2002}+\sqrt{2003}\right)^2.$$

The triangle $ABC$ is drawn on the Cartesian plane $xOy$. Both coordinates of all vertices of the triangle are integer numbers, and there are no interior points of the triangle (not on the contour) both coordinates of which are integer numbers. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ cannot be acute-angled.

$2003^2$ soldiers stand on the range, forming the square $2003\times2003$ ($2003$ columns with $2003$ soldiers each). There do not exist two men of the same height. Every minute the tallest soldier of each row and the shortest soldier of each column sit down (among those who did not sit down before). Soldiers who had sat down once do not take part in the process any more. The described process stops when all soldiers have sat down.
a) Find the maximum possible duration of the process.
b) Find the minimum possible duration of the process.

Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Find all real numbers $x$ such that
$$\sqrt{\frac{x^2}{3}-ax+a^2}+\sqrt{\frac{x^2}{3}-bx+b^2}=\sqrt{a^2-ab+b^2}.$$

Some $2n^2+3n+2$ cells ($n$ is a positive integer) of a square table $(2n+1)\times(2n+1)$ are marked. Does there always exist at least one three-cell figure shown below (such figures can be oriented arbitrarily), all three cells of which are marked?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ua9_2003_p7_fig.png

The rectangles $ABB_1A_1$, $BCC_1B_2$ and $ACC_2A_2$ are constructed internally on the sides of the triangle $ABC$ (for instance, for the rectangle $ABB_1A_1$ it means that the points $B_1$, $A_1$, $C$ all lie on one side of the line $AB$). Prove that the lines passing through the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ perpendicular to the lines $A_1A_2$, $B_1B_2$, $C_1C_2$ respectively are concurrent.
Prove that the equation $p^3-q^3=2004$ has no natural solutions.

Draw the set of points $(x,y)$ on the coordinate plane that satisfy the equality:
$$x^2-|x|=|y|.$$

Let $D$, $E$, $F$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ of triangle $ABC$ respectively, and let $H$, $G$ be the midpoints of $DE$, $DF$. Is it possible to put the digits from $1$ to $8$ into the points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$ in such a way that the sums of numbers on the sides of the triangle and on the lines $DE$, $DF$ are equal?

Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be positive reals such that $x+y+z=1$. Prove the inequality:
$$\sqrt{xy+z}+\sqrt{yz+x}+\sqrt{zx+y}\geqslant 1+\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx}.$$

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with base $AC$ and let $K$ be a point on the side $AB$. Under a rotation with center $K$ the point $A$ goes to the point $A_1$ that lies on the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$, and the point $A_1$ goes to the midpoint of $AC$. Construct the triangle $ABC$ if only the points $A_1$ and $B$ are given.

The bisector of an acute angle of a right triangle divides the opposite leg in the ratio $a:b$ (counting from the vertex of the acute angle to the vertex of the right angle), $a>b$. Find the ratio of the length of the bisector to the length of this leg.

Draw the set of points $(x,y)$ on the coordinate plane that satisfy the equation:
$$\{x\}^2+\{y\}^2=1.$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be real numbers such that $a+b
eq0$, $b+c
eq0$, $c+a
eq0$. Prove that the numbers $ rac{1}{b+c},  rac{1}{c+a},  rac{1}{a+b}$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression (in that order) if and only if the numbers $a^4+a^2b^2+b^4$, $a^4+a^2c^2+c^4$, $b^4+b^2c^2+c^4$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression (in that order).

Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{2004}\geqslant 0$ be real numbers such that $a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_{2004}\leqslant 25$. Prove that there exist indices $1\leqslant i<j\leqslant 2004$ such that $\left|\sqrt{a_i}-\sqrt{a_j}\right|\leqslant\frac{5}{2003}$.

There is a square $n\times n$ field divided into $n^2$ square plots $1\times1$, and there are $n$ farmers. At the beginning every farmer has $1$ plot, such that in every row and every column there is only one plot that belongs to some farmer. Every next day every farmer adds to his land a new plot that has a common side with the plot that he got one day before. If after $n$ days all plots have their owners, then this dividing process is called good. Prove that if $n=k^4$ for some odd $k$, then there is a good dividing process for this field.

a) Find all real $x$ such that the following equality holds:
$$x^2+\frac{1}{x^2+2x}=1.$$
b) Find all pairs of positive reals $x$, $y$ such that:
$$x^2+\frac{1}{x^2+2x}+y^2+\frac{1}{y^2+2y}=2.$$
Justify your answer.

Given the trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $BC$ and $AD$. Points $M$ and $N$ are chosen on $AB$ and $CD$ respectively such that $MN$ is parallel to $BC$ and passes through the intersection point of $AC$ and $BD$. Let $DP$, $AQ$ be the altitudes of the triangles $DMC$, $ABN$ respectively. Prove that $AP=DQ$.

Prove that for all positive $a$, $b$, $c$ the following inequality holds:
$$\left(\frac{a+b}{c^2}+\frac{b+c}{a^2}+\frac{c+a}{b^2}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{a^2}{b+c}+\frac{b^2}{c+a}+\frac{c^2}{a+b}\right)\geqslant 3+\frac{a+b}{c}+\frac{b+c}{a}+\frac{c+a}{b}.$$

The array $2006\times2006$ is filled arbitrarily with the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 2006^2$ such that each number occurs exactly once in the array. In one step it is allowed to choose some row and sort its numbers in increasing order from left to right, or to choose some column and sort its numbers in increasing order from top to bottom.
a) Is it possible that after some steps we will get the same array?
b) Prove that $4012$ steps are always enough to get an array in which all rows are sorted and all columns are sorted.
Find all natural numbers $a$, $100\leqslant a\leqslant 999$, such that $a^2$ and $(3a-2)^2$ have the same last three digits in the same order.

There are $11$ students, $11$ languages and a teacher. In one lesson the teacher can teach two students two languages (the two students will then know both of these languages). What is the least number of lessons necessary to teach all students all languages?

Given an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. Let $D$ be a variable point on the segment $BC$ ($D\neq B,C$), and let $P$ and $Q$ be the circumcenters of $ABD$ and $ACD$ respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles $APQ$ have a common point different from $A$.

Find all real $a$ such that the inequality
$$\left(ax^2+4(a+1)x+4a+1\right)\left((4a+1)x^2+4(a+1)x+a\right)\geqslant 0$$
holds for all real $x$.

There is a rook in the lower left corner of the board. The first player on his turn moves the rook up or down and the second player on his turn moves the rook right or left, such that the trajectory of the rook does not intersect itself. A player loses if he can't make a move. Who has a winning strategy if the size of the board is a) $2007\times2007$; b) $2006\times2007$ ($2006$ squares in the column)?

Find all pairs of natural numbers $m$, $n$ such that:
$$4^n+n\cdot2^{n+1}+2n^2=m^2+4.$$
Inside the triangle $ABC$ with $\angle C=90^\circ$, $\angle A=60^\circ$ there is a point $O$ such that $\angle AOB=120^\circ$, $OC=1$, $OB=4$. Find $AO$.
In the convex heptagon $ABCDEFG$, $AC\parallel EF$, $BD\parallel FG$, $CE\parallel GA$, $DF\parallel AB$, $EG\parallel BC$, $FA\parallel CD$. Prove that $GB\parallel DE$.

It is allowed to replace the ordered pair $(a,b)$ by $\left(a\pm\frac{2}{b},b\right)$ if $b\neq0$ or by $\left(a,b\pm\frac{2}{a}\right)$ if $a\neq0$.
a) Show a sequence of operations to obtain the pair $(2,-2007)$ from the pair $(2007,2)$.
b) Prove that for every such sequence there is a moment when we get a pair that contains $0$.

In a convex $2007$-gon all sides and diagonals are colored in one of $k$ colors. Every three vertices of the $2007$-gon form a triangle at least two sides of which have the same color. Find all $k$ for which this is possible.
It is known that $x^2+(y-4)^2=1$. Find the minimum and the maximum of $|x|+|y|$.

Prove that for positive reals $a$, $b$, $c$ the following inequality holds:
$$\frac{a+b}{2b+c}+\frac{b+c}{2c+a}+\frac{c+a}{2a+b}\geqslant 2.$$

The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. Prove that the three perpendiculars from the midpoints of $A_1B_1$, $B_1C_1$ and $C_1A_1$ to $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ respectively are concurrent.
It is known that for some natural $n$ the last digit of the number $n^3+2009n^2+27n$ is $3$. Find the last three digits of this number.

There are $n$ natural numbers on the board. It is allowed to write on the board only natural numbers of the form $\frac{a+b}{a-b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are on the board. Find all $n$ and all possible first $n$ numbers that are on the board such that it is possible to write each natural number on the board.

In the acute-angled triangle $ABC$, $BB_1$ is an altitude. The point $D$ is chosen on the side $BC$ such that $\angle BAD=\angle CBB_1$. The segments $AD$ and $BB_1$ intersect at $F$. The perpendicular from $B$ to $AB$ intersects $CF$ at $K$. Prove that $DK$ passes through the midpoint of $BF$.

Peter has some equal white $4\times4$ squares. He paints each cell of each square black or blue in such a way that no two different squares have equal $i$-th rows or equal $i$-th columns, $1\leqslant i\leqslant4$. What is the greatest number of squares that Peter can paint?
In the coordinate plane $xOy$, depict the set of all points such that $|y-[x]|=2-y-[x]$, where $[x]$ is the integer part of $x$, i.e. the largest integer $n\leqslant x$.

Let $f(x)=\frac{x^3}{3x^2-3x+1}$. Compute
$$f\left(\frac{1}{2012}\right)+f\left(\frac{2}{2012}\right)+\cdots+f\left(\frac{2012}{2012}\right).$$
For a triangle $ABC$, $I_A$ is the center of the excircle opposite the vertex $A$. Prove that the points $B$, $C$ and the circumcenters of the triangles $ABI_A$ and $ACI_A$ are concyclic.

Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that it is possible to fill all cells of a table $n\times n$ with integers from the interval $[-30,30]$ so that:
1) each integer from this interval is written,
2) no column and no row contains two numbers with negative product.
Positive numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the equation $x^2+y^2+\frac{8xy}{x+y}=16$. Prove that $x+y=4$.

In a triangle $ABC$, $\angle C=90^\circ$, $AC<BC$. The point $K$ inside $BC$ is such that $CK=CA$, and the point $D$ inside $CK$ is such that $\angle DAK=\angle BAK$. $F$ and $P$ are, respectively, the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and from $A$ to $FK$. Prove that $CP=\frac{1}{2}(AF+FD+DA)$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $\frac{a^4-1}{b+1}+\frac{b^4-1}{a+1}$ is an integer. Prove that $a^{2010}b^{2012}-1$ is divisible by $a+1$.

There are $2012$ cities in the land of Olympia. Some of the cities are connected by direct two-way routes (each route connects exactly two cities and no two routes connect the same pair of cities). It is known that no city is directly connected to more than $8$ other cities. Prove that it is possible to close at most $2012$ routes in such a way that among any four cities there will be two with no direct route between them.

Two circles $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ of the same radius meet at the points $A$ and $B$. The circle $\gamma$ with centre at the point $A$ meets the circle $\gamma_1$ at the points $C$ and $D$. Prove that the points of intersection of the circles $\gamma$ and $\gamma_2$ belong to the lines $BC$ and $BD$.

Andrii and Olesia play the following game. First Andrii places all 10 digits around a circle. After that Olesia chooses a digit, and from this digit she moves around the circle clockwise, grouping the digits consecutively in pairs. In this way 5 two-digit numbers are formed (a number like 06 is also taken into account, as the one-digit number 6). After that Olesia adds these 5 numbers and wins the resulting sum from Andrii. What is the smallest loss Andrii can guarantee for himself?
Let $a, b>0$ be real numbers. It is known that $\left(a^2+b^2\right)(a-b+1)\ge b$. Prove that $a(a+b)\ge b$.

What is the largest number of corners of three cells (see the figure) that can be placed inside a $7\times 7$ grid square so that they pairwise do not touch each other along sides? (Touching at corners is allowed.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ua9_2014_1_p4_fig.png
For which natural $n$ do there exist numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ satisfying the conditions $$a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n>0\quad\text{and}\quad a_1^3+a_2^3+\ldots+a_n^3<0?$$

A terrain is divided into squares forming a large $5\times 5$ square. In some of the small squares there are mines (at most one per square), but it is not known in which squares exactly they are located. The captain of a group of sappers has a plan of the terrain: a $5\times 5$ square in whose cells numbers are written showing how many of the neighbouring squares of the corresponding square of the terrain contain a mine (the presence of a mine in the given square itself is not counted). Squares having a common vertex or a common side are considered neighbouring. Can the captain always determine the total number of mines on the whole field?

Maksym is guessing a natural number $n$ about which he knows that it has exactly 250 natural divisors $1=d_1<d_2<\ldots<d_{250}=n$. In one move Maksym may name some index $j$, $1\le j\le 249$, and learn the value $d_j$. However, he is forbidden to ask for $d_j$ if he already knows $d_{251-j}$. What is the minimal number of moves in which Maksym can be sure to guess the number $n$?

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $w_1$; $AN$ and $CK$ are its altitudes and $H$ is the orthocentre. The circle $w_2$ circumscribed about $\triangle NBK$ meets the circle $w_1$ for the second time at the point $P$. The lines $CA$ and $BP$ meet at the point $S$. The line $SH$ meets the circle $w_2$ for the second time at the point $Q$. Prove that the lines $NQ$, $PK$ and $CA$ meet at one point or are parallel.

It is known that for numbers $a, b, c$ the following condition holds: the arithmetic mean of the numbers $a, b$ equals the number $c$, that is, $c=\frac12(a+b)$, and the geometric mean of the numbers $a, c$ equals the number $b$, that is, $b=\sqrt{ac}$. Must the numbers $a, b, c$ be equal to one another?

In a triangle $ABC$ the points $A_1$ and $C_1$ are chosen on the sides $BC$ and $AB$ respectively such that $AA_1=CC_1$. The segments $AA_1$ and $CC_1$ meet at the point $F$. It turned out that $\angle CFA_1=2\angle ABC$. Prove that $AA_1=AC$.
Find all primes $p<q<r$ such that the numbers $A=(r-p)(r-q)(q-p)+1$ and $B=3p+5q$ are equal to one and the same prime number.

There are $2k+1$ people, all of pairwise different heights. Denote their heights in increasing order, from the shortest to the tallest, as follows: $a_1<a_2<\ldots<a_{2k+1}$. After that they are lined up in an arbitrary way in the form of an $M\times N$ table ($M$ rows and $N$ columns). Now in each of the $M$ rows we choose the person who is the middle one by height. And then from these $M$ people who are middle by height we choose the one who is the middle one by height, whom we call the median person.

a) What is the smallest height the median person can have if $2k+1=2015$?

b) What is the smallest height the median person can have for an arbitrary $k$?

The bisector of the angle $\angle ABC$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle at the point $K$. The point $N$ belongs to the segment $AB$, and $NK\perp AB$. Through the point $P$, the midpoint of the segment $NB$, a line parallel to the line $BC$ is drawn; it meets the line $BK$ at the point $T$. Prove that the line $NT$ bisects the segment $AC$.
For positive numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ satisfying the condition $$x_1^{n-1}+x_2^{n-1}+\ldots+x_n^{n-1}=x_1x_2\ldots x_n,$$ prove the inequality $$(x_1-n+1)(x_2-n+1)\ldots(x_n-n+1)\ge 1.$$

For some odd $n$ an $n\times n$ square is divided into $n^2$ cells, and in one of its cells there lie $n^2$ counters. In one step it is allowed to move two counters from a cell containing at least two counters into the cells that are symmetric with respect to this cell and have at least one common point with it. There are four types of such moves: type (1): the counters are moved parallel to the vertical; type (2): parallel to the horizontal; type (3): parallel to the diagonal of the square going from the lower left corner to the upper right one; type (4): parallel to the other diagonal of the square. After several steps it turned out that every cell of the square contains exactly one counter. Prove that the number of moves of type (3) made is the same as the number of moves of type (4).
It is known that the numbers $a, b, c$ satisfy the conditions $$\frac{a+c}{a+1}=b,\quad \frac{c+b}{c+1}=a,\quad \frac{b+a}{b+1}=c.$$ What values can the expression $(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)$ take?

The numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$ are written in a row. The numbers 1 and $n$ are coloured blue, and all the others yellow. Two players, Olesia and Andrii, take turns colouring one of the yellow numbers blue according to the following rules: with the first move Olesia (she starts) colours any of the yellow numbers blue (denote it by $k$). Then Andrii chooses that one of the intervals of numbers $(1, 2, \ldots, k)$ or $(k, k+1, \ldots, n)$ which contains more yellow numbers. If these intervals contain the same number of yellow numbers, either of the two intervals is chosen. If, for example, the larger interval is $(1, 2, \ldots, k)$, then the other interval takes no further part in the game. After that Andrii colours blue any of the yellow numbers of the new interval. Now the new interval has also been divided into two smaller ones. Then Olesia, for her move, chooses that one of the two new intervals which contains more yellow numbers, and the other interval is out of the game. And so on. The winner of the game is the player who manages to colour blue a number whose neighbours on the left and on the right are already blue. Who wins this game with correct play of both players?

A triangle $ABC$ is given in which $AB>AC$. Through the point $A$ the tangent to the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$ is drawn. This tangent meets the line $BC$ at the point $P$. On the extension of the side $BA$ beyond the point $A$ the point $Q$ is marked such that $AQ=AC$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the midpoints of the segments $CQ$ and $AP$ respectively, and let $R$ be a point of the segment $AP$ such that $AR=CP$. Prove that $CR=2XY$.

For which natural $n$ do there exist $2n$ pairwise distinct natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ and $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ satisfying the equalities $$a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n=b_1+b_2+\ldots+b_n\quad\text{and}\quad a_1a_2\ldots a_n=b_1b_2\ldots b_n?$$
Positive numbers $a, b$ satisfy the condition $ab=1$. Prove that the inequality $$\frac{3a+1}{b+1}+\frac{3b+1}{a+1}\ge 4$$ holds. For which pairs $(a, b)$ is equality possible?

$n$ cells, numbered from left to right with the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$, are drawn on the board. In each cell the sign "$+$" is written. Andriiko has to make $n$ moves. With the first move he changes the sign to the opposite one in one arbitrary cell of his choice. With the second move, in two arbitrary neighbouring cells, then in three neighbouring cells, and so on. With the penultimate move he changes the sign in $n-1$ cells, and with the last move he changes the sign in all $n$ cells. For which $n$ can Andriiko obtain the sign "$-$" in all cells at the end of the process?

For what largest natural $n\ge 3$ does there exist

a) a convex $n$-gon,

b) an arbitrary $n$-gon,

whose angles satisfy the following conditions:

- they are measured by an integer number of degrees;

- the ratio of any two angles (the larger to the smaller) is a natural number greater than one?

The segment $AB$ is a diameter of a circle $w$, and $CD$ is a chord of this circle perpendicular to $AB$. The point $O$ is the centre of the circle $w$. Through the point $E$, the midpoint of the segment $CO$, the line $AE$ is drawn, which meets the circle $w$ for the second time at the point $F$. The segment $BC$ meets the segment $AF$ at the point $M$, and the segment $DF$ at the point $L$. The circumcircle of $\triangle DLM$ meets the circle $w$ for the second time at the point $K$. Prove that $KM=MB$.

Natural numbers $k$ and $N$ satisfy the condition $$N\cdot(N+1)\cdot\ldots\cdot(N+k)=6\,952\,862\,280.$$ Find all possible values of $k$ and $N$ if it is known that the last digit of the number $N$ is 1.

Let $w_1, w_2$ be two circles in the plane that do not intersect. The line $AB$ is their common external tangent, $O$ is the point of intersection of the common internal tangents, and $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from $O$ to $AB$. From the point $H$ the tangents $HC$, $HD$ to the circles $w_1, w_2$ respectively, different from $AB$, are drawn. Prove that $HO$ is the bisector of $\angle CHD$.

The number 2017 is written on the board. At each step we add one more natural number to the board so that the following conditions hold: the arithmetic mean of all numbers written on the board at the given moment must be a natural number and less than the arithmetic mean computed at the previous step. What is the largest number of numbers we can write on the board, counting the initial one?

A natural number $n\ge 3$ is given. Olesia plays the following game: at the beginning of the game a counter is located at the origin of the Cartesian plane $XOY$. Olesia moves the counter according to the following rules: the counter may be moved in the plane only parallel to the coordinate axes. At the first step the counter must be moved by the distance $1=2^0$, at the second step by the distance $2=2^1$, at the third step by the distance $4=2^2$, and so on (the displacement of the counter at each new step is twice as long as at the previous step). In total Olesia makes $n$ steps. Her loss in this game equals the maximal distance from the counter to the origin during the whole game (not necessarily after the $n$-th step). What is the smallest loss Olesia can achieve?

60 participants took part in an olympiad. They were offered 8 problems, each of which was marked from 0 to 7 points. Prove that in the final standings there must be 3 participants whose results differ pairwise by at most 1 point. Would the statement of the problem remain true if 58 participants took part in the olympiad?

The result of a participant in the olympiad is the total number of points he scored.

During April Andrii read a thick book. He read it according to the following schedule: from 1 to 20 April he read on average $20$ pages per day, from 6 to 25 April he read on average $30$ pages per day, and from 11 to 30 April he read on average $40$ pages per day. What are the largest and the smallest possible numbers of pages in this book?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the bisector of angle $A$ meets the circumcircle of this triangle at the point $W$. From the point $W$ the perpendicular $WU$ is dropped to the line $AB$, and from the incentre $I$ of the same triangle the perpendicular $IP$ is dropped to the line $WU$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the segment $BC$. Prove that the line $MP$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $CI$.

The divisors of a composite natural number $n$ which is not the square of a prime are denoted, in increasing order, by $1<d_1<d_2<\ldots<d_{l-1}<d_l<n$, $l\ge 2$. For which $n$ do there exist natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $N$ satisfying the conditions $d_1+d_2=N^a$ and $d_{l-1}+d_l=N^b$?

For a natural number $n$ denote by $S(n)$ the sum of its digits. Among all pairs of natural numbers $(n, m)$ satisfying the equality $S(n)\cdot S(n+1)\cdot\ldots\cdot S(n+m)=2018$, find the one for which the sum $n+m$ takes the smallest possible value.

In a triangle $ABC$ the points $M_1, M_2, M_3$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC, AC, AB$ respectively. The point $K$ is symmetric to $M_2$ with respect to the line $BC$, and $AH$ is an altitude of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the line $KM_3$ bisects the segment $HM_1$.
Prove that for positive numbers $x, y, z$ the inequality $$\frac13\left(x^3+y^3+z^3\right)\ge xyz+\frac29(x+y+z)(x-z)^2$$ holds.

A round tower has $16$ doors, behind each of which a chest with Captain Flint's gold is hidden. The doors are placed around the perimeter of the tower at equal distances between neighbouring ones and are numbered clockwise with the numbers from 1 to 16. $16$ pirates came up to the tower, each of whom has one key, and all the keys are numbered with the numbers from 1 to 16. It is known that the key with number $n$ opens the door with number $m$ if and only if $m$ is divisible by $n$. The pirates stand one at each door, but they do not know the number of the door at which they are standing. Jim Hawkins knows which pirate has which key and wants them to take as few chests of gold as possible. Jim can rotate the tower so that the doors in front of the pirates are arranged as he wishes, but the door numbers still go consecutively around the circle clockwise $1$–$16$, starting from some door. What is the largest number of chests of gold that the pirates are certain to be able to take under these conditions?

A natural number $n>1$ is given. $2019$ natural numbers are placed around a circle. It is known that the product of any two neighbouring ones among them is an exact $n$-th power of some natural number. Is it necessarily true that the product of any two (not necessarily neighbouring) of these numbers is also an exact $n$-th power of a natural number?

Let the point $M$ be the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AB$ of a right triangle $ABC$. The perpendicular bisector of the hypotenuse $AB$ meets the leg $BC$ at the point $K$. The perpendicular drawn from the point $K$ to the line $CM$ meets the extension of the segment $AC$ beyond the point $A$ at the point $P$. The lines $CM$ and $BP$ meet at the point $T$. Prove that $AC=TB$.

In a company of people there are no three people who are pairwise acquainted with each other, and among any five people there are three who have a common acquaintance. Prove that the people can be split into two groups of pairwise unacquainted people.

The polynomial $x^2+1$ is written on the board. Every day Katia erases the polynomial $F(x)$ written on the board and writes instead of it one of the two polynomials $F^2(x)+1$ or $F(x^2+1)$. Prove that after a year the constant term of the polynomial written on the board will be greater than $2^{2^{222}}$.

The natural numbers $a<b$ are written on the board. At each step two numbers written on the board are erased and their sum and the absolute value of their difference are written instead. At some moment the number $2019$ appeared written on the board. For what smallest possible $b$ is this possible?
Prove that for arbitrary real $x, y, z$ the inequality $$x^2\left(3y^2+3z^2-2yz\right)\ge yz(2xy+2xz-yz)$$ holds. For which triples can equality be attained?
Natural numbers $a, b, c$ are given. Prove that there exists an integer $k\ge 0$ for which $$\gcd\left(a^k+bc,\ b^k+ca,\ c^k+ab\right)>1.$$

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $w$ with centre at the point $O$. The extensions of its altitudes drawn from the vertices $A$ and $C$ meet $w$ for the second time at the points $A_0$ and $C_0$ respectively. The line $A_0C_0$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at the points $A_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. The points $A_2$ and $C_2$ on the side $AC$ are such that $A_2O\parallel BC$ and $C_2O\parallel AB$. Let $H$ be the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$ and $T$ the point of intersection of $A_1A_2$ and $C_1C_2$. Prove that $HT\parallel AC$.
What is the largest number of numbers that can be chosen among the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 2n$ so that any two of them have a common divisor greater than $1$?

An equilateral triangle with side $n$ is divided into $n^2$ small equilateral triangles with side length 1 (see the figure). At the very beginning one of them, which has no common points with the outer sides of the big triangle, was coloured blue, and the rest yellow. In one move one may choose any of the $n^2$ small triangles and change its colour and the colours of the triangles adjacent to it along a side (from blue to yellow and vice versa). Is it possible after several moves to make the whole board one-coloured?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ua9_2020_1_p2_fig.png

Prove that for every natural $n>1$ there exists a sequence of natural numbers $a_1\le a_2\le\ldots\le a_m=n$, $m>1$, such that $$5\left(a_1^2+a_2^2+\ldots+a_m^2\right)-4\left(a_1a_2+a_2a_3+\ldots+a_{m-1}a_m\right)\le 4n^2+\frac12(m+1).$$

In a triangle $ABC$ the orthocentre $H$ is the midpoint of the altitude $AD$, and $O$ is the circumcentre of $\triangle ABC$. The line passing through the point $H$ perpendicular to the line $HO$ meets the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of $\triangle ABC$ at the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Prove that the midpoints of the segments $BP$, $CQ$ and the point $O$ lie on one line.
For natural numbers $a\ge b\ge c\ge d$ prove the inequality $$ab+bc+cd-b^2-c^2-d^2\ge a-d.$$

Let a quadrilateral $ABCD$ be circumscribed about a circle with centre at the point $O$. On the rays $AB$, $AD$, $CB$ and $CD$ equal segments $AA_1$, $AA_2$, $CC_1$ and $CC_2$ are laid off, whose length is greater than the length of any of the sides of the quadrilateral $ABCD$. It turned out that the points $A_1$, $A_2$, $C_1$ and $C_2$ lie on one circle with centre at the point $O$. Prove that the lines $A_1A_2$, $C_1C_2$ and $BD$ meet at one point or are parallel.

There are 4 countries, each of which has several cities. Between the cities of any two different countries at least $\frac56$ of the total possible number of roads between these countries have been built. Prove that one can choose one city from each country so that any two of these four cities are connected by a road. Between any two cities at most one road can be built.

For which natural $n>1$ does there exist a set of pairwise distinct natural numbers $(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ for which the condition $$(a_1+1)!+(a_2+1)!+\ldots+(a_n+1)!\ \vdots\ a_1!+a_2!+\ldots+a_n!$$ holds (that is, the left-hand side is divisible by the right-hand side)?

Oleksii and Bohdan play a game with two piles of pebbles. At the beginning one of the piles contains 2021 pebbles, and the other is empty. In one move each of the boys must take an even number of stones (greater than zero) from an arbitrary pile, after which he moves half of the taken pebbles to the other pile and removes the other half from the game. The player who cannot make a move loses. Who wins this game if both strive to win and Bohdan starts?
Prove that there exist distinct natural numbers $a$ and $b$, greater than $1000000$, such that $\left(a^b+1\right)$ is divisible by $\left(b^a+1\right)$.

Non-negative numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ are such that $x_1^2+x_2^2+\ldots+x_n^2=n$, $n>1$. Prove that for arbitrary non-negative real numbers $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ there exist indices $i, j\in\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, not necessarily distinct, for which the inequality $x_i+y_j-x_{j+1}y_{i+1}\ge 1$ holds (the index $n+1\equiv 1$).

A triangle $ABC$ with $\angle A=60^\circ$ is given. On the sides $AB$ and $AC$ the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively are marked such that $BP=PQ=QC$. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ passes through the projection of the orthocentre of the triangle $ABC$ onto its median drawn to the side $BC$.

Denote by $M$ the set consisting of the natural numbers that can be represented in the form $(a+b)\left(a^2+b^2\right)$, where $a, b$ are some distinct natural numbers. Prove that for arbitrary natural numbers $n>k$ the number $n^4-k^4$ is the sum of some $n-k$ pairwise distinct elements of the set $M$.

Circles $w_1$ and $w_2$ meet at the points $P$ and $Q$ and are internally tangent to a circle $w$ with centre at the point $O$ at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. It is known that the points $A$, $B$ and $Q$ lie on one line. Prove that the point $O$ lies on the external bisector of $\angle APB$.

$100$ children from $10$ regions of Ukraine, $10$ children from each region, came to the all-Ukrainian mathematical olympiad. At the opening they stood in one row on the stage, but not all children from the same region stood next to each other. Two neighbouring children from different regions can be swapped in 1 second. What is the smallest time in which one can guarantee to make the children line up by regions (the regions may follow in an arbitrary order)?

For an arbitrary natural $a>1$ define the sequence $(a_n)$ as follows: $a_{n+1}=a_n+d(a_n)-1$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $a_1=a$, where $d(b)$ denotes the smallest prime divisor of the number $b$. Prove that for every natural $k$ the sequence $d(a_n)$ for $n\ge k$ is not increasing, that is, the condition $d(a_{n+1})\ge d(a_n)$ does not hold for all $n\ge k$.

$n\ge 4$ real numbers are placed around a circle. It is known that for any four consecutive numbers $a, b, c, d$ going around the circle in this order the condition $a+d=b+c$ holds. For which $n$ can one conclude that all the numbers are equal?

Natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{101}$ are such that $a_i+1$ is divisible by $a_{i+1}$ for $1\le i\le 101$ (we assume that $a_{102}=a_1$). What is the largest value that the maximum of these numbers can take?

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with circumcircle $\omega$ is given. Points $F$ on $AC$, $E$ on $AB$ and $P$, $Q$ on $\omega$ are such that $\angle AFB=\angle AEC=\angle APE=\angle AQF=90^\circ$. Prove that the lines $BC$, $EF$ and $PQ$ meet at one point.

Find the smallest real number $C$ for which the following condition holds: for arbitrary distinct natural numbers $x, y$ the inequality $$\min\left\{\left\{\sqrt{x^2+2y}\right\},\left\{\sqrt{y^2+2x}\right\}\right\}<C$$ holds.

Here $\{a\}\in[0;1)$ denotes the fractional part of the number $a$, that is, there is an integer $n$ for which the equality $a=n+\{a\}$ holds. For example, $\{3.14\}=0.14$.
Do there exist $10$ numbers, not all of which are equal, each of which equals the square of the sum of all the other numbers?

Inside a triangle $ABC$ there is a point $O$ such that $\angle BOC=90^\circ-\angle BAC$. The rays $BO$ and $CO$ meet the sides $AC$ and $AB$ at the points $K$ and $L$ respectively. The points $K_1$ and $L_1$ are chosen on the segments $LC$ and $BK$ respectively so that $BK_1=K_1K$ and $CL_1=L_1L$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. Prove that $\angle K_1ML_1$ is a right angle.
$n\ge 2$ pairwise distinct natural numbers are given. Call a pair of numbers elegant if their sum is a natural power of two. For each $n$ find the largest possible number of elegant pairs.

What is the largest number of edges that a graph on $2n$ vertices can have if there is exactly one way to split its vertices into $n$ pairs in such a way that in each pair the vertices are joined by an edge?

Oleksii wrote on the board several pairwise distinct natural numbers and computed all sums of pairs of distinct numbers. It turned out that among the last digits of all these sums all digits from 0 to 9 occur. What is the smallest possible number of numbers Oleksii wrote down?

For some natural number $n$ consider an $n\times n$ board. One may place on this board arbitrary rectangles whose sides go along the grid lines. What is the smallest number of such rectangles that must be placed so that all cells of the board are covered by different numbers of rectangles (including the case of not being covered by any of the rectangles)? The rectangles placed on the board may have equal dimensions.

2024 positive real numbers with sum 1 are placed around a circle. It is known that any two neighbouring numbers differ by at least a factor of two. For each of the 2024 pairs of neighbouring numbers the smaller was subtracted from the larger, after which all these 2024 differences were added. What is the smallest value this sum can take?

On the lateral sides $AC$ and $AB$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ the points $E$ and $F$ respectively are chosen so that $AE=BF$. The point $D$ is chosen on the same side of the line $EF$ as the point $A$ in such a way that the triangles $DFE$ and $ABC$ are similar. The line $EF$ meets the line $BC$ at some point $K$. Prove that the line $DK$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$.
For arbitrary real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ from the interval $[0;1]$ find the largest possible value of the expression $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2-ab-bc-cd-ad$.

A convex hexagon with parallel opposite sides is given. For each pair of opposite sides the line parallel to these sides and equidistant from them is constructed. Prove that the three lines obtained in this way meet at one point if and only if the lengths of opposite sides are equal.
Find all composite odd numbers all of whose divisors can be split into pairs so that the sum of the numbers in each pair is a power of two, each divisor belonging to exactly one such pair.
Solve the system of equations $$\begin{cases}y=x^2+2x,\\ z=y^2+2y,\\ x=z^2+2z.\end{cases}$$

On the side $AC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ arbitrary points $D$ and $E$ are chosen. The circumcircles of the triangles $BDC$ and $BEA$ meet the sides $BA$ and $BC$ respectively for the second time at the points $F$ and $G$. The point $O$ is the circumcentre of $\triangle BFG$. Prove that $OD=OE$.

Anton wrote 4 natural numbers on the board. Oleksii computed their product, and Fedir the sum of their fourth powers. Can Oleksii's number and Fedir's number have the same number of digits, these numbers being written with the digits in reverse order with respect to each other?

There are $n^2+n$ numbers, among which no number occurs more than $\frac{n^2+n}{2}$ times. Prove that they can be split into $(n+1)$ groups of $n$ numbers so that the sums of the numbers in these groups are pairwise distinct.

Oleksii has the following grid of 7 hexagonal cells (see the figure). Initially the number 1 is written in the central cell, and the number 0 in the others. In one operation Oleksii may choose an arbitrary cell and either add 1 to all numbers in the cells adjacent to it along a side, or subtract 1 from all such numbers (the number in the cell itself does not change). Can Oleksii make the numbers in all cells equal to 0?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ua9_2025_2_p5_fig.png

The sum of 10 natural numbers equals $300$. The product of their factorials is an exact tenth power of some natural number. Prove that all 10 numbers are equal to one another.

For a natural number $n$, its factorial $n!$ is the product of all natural numbers from $1$ to $n$.

In a quadrilateral $ABCD$ it is known that $\angle ABC=\angle ADC=90^\circ$. On the ray $AB$ beyond the point $B$ a point $K$ is chosen such that $\angle AKD=\angle ADB$. The point $L$ is the projection of the point $K$ onto the line $AD$, and the point $N$ is the projection of the point $D$ onto the line $CL$. Find the degree measure of $\angle ANK$.
$2025$ pairwise distinct natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2025}$ are given. Find the largest possible number of equal numbers among the fractions of the form $\frac{a_i^2+a_j^2}{a_i+a_j}$.

Numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are given, each of which has exactly 2026 non-zero digits after the decimal point. Denote by $x_{(n)}$ the rounding of the number $x$, according to the rounding rules, to the $n$-th digit after the decimal point, for $n=1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2026$. Can it happen that:

a) $a_{(1)}+b_{(1)}>c_{(1)}+d_{(1)}$, $a_{(2)}+b_{(2)}<c_{(2)}+d_{(2)}$ and $a_{(3)}+b_{(3)}>c_{(3)}+d_{(3)}$?

b) for even $n$ the inequality $a_{(n)}+b_{(n)}<c_{(n)}+d_{(n)}$ holds, and for odd $n$ the inequality $a_{(n)}+b_{(n)}>c_{(n)}+d_{(n)}$ holds?

In a trapezoid $ABCD$ the point of intersection of the diagonals $Q$ is marked, the points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ respectively, and the point $P$ lies on the base $AD$ so that $PB=PC$. Prove that the triangles $PMN$ and $QBC$ are similar.

Rostyk and Slavko play a game, making moves in turn; Rostyk starts. At the beginning the number 3 is written on the board. In one move one must erase the written number $a$ and write instead one of three numbers: $a+1$, $a+2$ or $ka$, where $k\ge 2$ is a natural number chosen by the player at his discretion on each move. One of the players wins if after his opponent's move a number greater than $2026$ is written on the board for the first time. Which of the players can guarantee himself the win?

Let a natural number $c$ be given. Consider all sequences of natural numbers $(a_n)$ such that for every natural number $n$ the equality $a_{n+2}=\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_n)+c$ holds. Find all natural numbers $a$ such that among these sequences there is one in which the number $a$ occurs infinitely many times.

What is the largest number of $1\times 1$ cells that can be marked on a $10\times 10$ board so that for every marked cell the following condition holds: among the distances from the centre of this cell to the centres of all other marked cells there is one that is strictly smaller than all the others?
Prove that there are infinitely many natural numbers that cannot be represented in the form $\gcd\left(m^n+1, n^m+1\right)$ for some natural numbers $m, n$.
Prove that for positive numbers $a>b>c$ the inequality $$\frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{(a+b-2c)^2}+\frac{b^2+bc+c^2}{(b+c-2a)^2}\le\frac{a^2+ac+c^2}{4(a-b)(b-c)}$$ holds.

On the sides $AB$, $AC$, $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ the points $E$, $F$, $D$ respectively are chosen so that $\angle DEF=\angle ACB$ and $\angle DFE=\angle ABC$. The points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ in such a way that $AP\parallel BC$ and $DP=DQ$. Prove that the points $A, E, F, Q$ lie on one circle.
